title: Measuring What Matters: Synthetic Benchmarks for Concept Bottleneck Models
claim: Letting humans verify uncertain inputs raises the share of cases a model can handle autonomously at a fixed accuracy target.
layout: 1 plot, selective accuracy vs coverage, shaded band, dashed arrows showing auto/ask/human splits
description: A single line plot with coverage (0–100%) on the x-axis and selective accuracy (80–100%) on the y-axis. A blue curve labeled CBM and a green curve labeled CBM + intervention both fall from the top left, and the green curve stays higher. A horizontal dashed black line marks the accuracy target, α_target, near 99%. Each curve crosses it at a dot: the blue dot is at 20% coverage and the green dot at 40%. A pale yellow vertical band between 20% and 40% marks the extra coverage gained from intervention. Below the curves, dashed double-headed arrows split coverage into segments. The green row reads auto, ask, human. The blue row reads auto, human. The eye goes first to the two crossing dots and the shaded gap between them.
caption: Interventions increase the work a model automates at a fixed selective-accuracy target αtarget. A CBM that abstains (blue) automates 20% of instances at the target and defers the rest to a human. When humans verify concepts where the model is uncertain ( shaded ), coverage grows to 40% (green).
abstract: Concept bottleneck models predict using high-level concepts detected in inputs. Although these models provide a simple way to reap benefits from interpretability, they are hard to train and evaluate because very few real-world datasets include concept labels. In this paper, we develop synthetic benchmarks for concept bottleneck models. With our benchmarks, researchers can generate labeled datasets and control properties that affect performance, such as data modality, the choice of concepts, or annotation quality. They can thus find problems that suit these models and isolate the factors behind their failures. We demonstrate how our benchmarks can be used to evaluate major use cases for concept bottleneck models: decision support, i.e., helping human experts make better decisions; and automation, i.e., handling routine tasks without supervision. Our demonstrations show how the benchmarks can identify new failure modes and attribute them to either the architecture or the data.
